# METHODOLOGY

This chapter explains how the study answers its research questions. It describes how the posts are collected and annotated, how the models are trained and compared, and how the benchmarking system and the prototype web application are built and tested.

## Research Methodology

This study follows the Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM) of Peffers et al. [-@peffers2007design]. Design science research creates and evaluates artifacts intended to solve identified problems [@peffers2007design]. The methodology fits this study because its main contribution is an artifact, a multi-task model that performs humanitarian classification and NER on Taglish typhoon posts. The dataset on which the model is trained, a set of Taglish typhoon posts annotated for both tasks, is a second artifact.

DSRM consists of six activities, and the study carries them out in order [@peffers2007design]. The first two, identifying the problem and defining the objectives of a solution, are presented in Chapter 1. The third is design and development. In this activity, the dataset is built, the multi-task model is designed, and one of 13 multi-task optimizers is selected on the validation set. The model trained with the selected optimizer is the final model. The fourth activity is demonstration, in which the final model is used in a prototype web application. The fifth is evaluation, in which the final model is compared on the test set with two single-task models, one for each task. The agreement between the annotators is also measured to check how consistently the dataset is annotated. The sixth is communication. The results are reported in this thesis, and the final model, the code, and the post IDs of the dataset are released.

## Subjects of the Study

The subjects of this study are the dataset, the multi-task model, and the two single-task models that serve as baselines. The dataset consists of about 2,500 Taglish posts on X about the tropical cyclones of January to November 2026. Each post is given one of the ten humanitarian categories of HumAID [@alam2021humaid], listed in @tbl-categories. The entity spans in the post are marked with the ten entity types of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner], listed in @tbl-entity-types. HUMAID-NER uses the same categories and entity types, so each F1-score of this study has a counterpart in HUMAID-NER. The comparison is only approximate, because HUMAID-NER is in English, is much larger, and has a similar number of posts in each category (Section 1.8).

The multi-task model follows the design of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. A single pretrained transformer encoder reads the post, and two task heads use its output, one to assign the humanitarian category and one to mark the entity spans (@fig-artifact). Each head is trained with a cross-entropy loss. This design is hard parameter sharing (Section 2.2). The encoder is SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, which is chosen because it was pretrained on 13 languages, including English and Filipino [@aisingapore2026sealion].

The multi-task model is trained with 13 multi-task optimizers, listed in @tbl-optimizers. Each optimizer gives one candidate model, so there are 13 candidate models. The optimizers are selected using two criteria. First, an optimizer must have been evaluated in at least two of the seven empirical studies of multi-task optimizers reviewed in Chapter 2. Requiring two studies limits the comparison to well-established optimizers, following Kurin et al. [-@kurin2022unitary]. Second, an optimizer must be trainable with the same model and training setup as the others, so that the optimizer is the only difference among the candidate models. No other optimizer meets both criteria.

Each single-task model is trained on one task alone. It uses the same encoder as the candidate models and the same task head and loss for its task. In total, 15 models are trained, the 13 candidate models and the two single-task models.

## Sampling Technique

The sampling frame consists of the posts on X that match the search keywords and fall within the collection window of a tropical cyclone. Each window starts one day before the tropical cyclone entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility and ends three days after it left. The dates of entry and exit are taken from the preliminary tropical cyclone reports of PAGASA [-@pagasa2026prelim]. The window extends beyond these dates because people also post about a tropical cyclone before it arrives and after it leaves. Zou et al. [-@zou2025typhoon] likewise collected posts from two days before to four days after landfall. Fewer extra days are added in this study because a tropical cyclone is already approaching the country while it is within the Philippine Area of Responsibility.

The search keywords are *bagyo* (tropical cyclone), *baha* (flood), and words formed from these two Tagalog roots, such as *bagyong* and *pagbaha* (@tbl-keyword-forms). The search function of X compares a keyword with the separate words of a post [@x2026operators]. A search for *bagyo* therefore does not return a post that contains only *bagyong*, so every word form is searched as a separate keyword. Storm names are not used as keywords, because many local storm names are also personal names and match far more posts than the keywords do (@tbl-storm-names).

A post is included when it contains at least one English word and at least one Tagalog word. The language of each word is identified with the dictionary-based method of Herrera et al. [-@herrera2022tweettaglish], which was developed for Taglish posts on X. One word of each language is enough, because any higher minimum would be arbitrary.

Reposts, quotes, and duplicates are excluded. A repost repeats a post that is already in the frame, and a quote includes text written by another user. Exact and near duplicates repeat the same text, which would then be counted more than once and could appear in both the training set and the test set. Duplicates are identified with the method of HumAID [@alam2021humaid], which measures how much wording two posts share (@tbl-duplicate-steps). When the similarity of two posts exceeds 0.75, only one of them is kept. HumAID adopted this threshold from @alam2021crisisbench, who set it after manually checking posts at several thresholds.

About 2,500 posts are drawn for annotation by proportionate stratified random sampling. Each day is a stratum, and it contributes posts in proportion to its number of matching posts. Simple random sampling would require the full list of matching posts, which is too costly to retrieve. Stratifying by humanitarian category is not possible either, because the category of a post is known only after annotation. The sample is limited to about 2,500 posts because that is the most that two annotators can complete at 2 to 3 hours a day over the 38 working days from December 2026 to January 2027. This is a sample size based on resource constraints [@lakens2022sample].

The annotated posts are divided into a training set (72%), a validation set (14%), and a test set (14%), following the proportions of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. Every model is trained, validated, and tested on the same posts, so that differences between models cannot come from differences in the posts. The split is stratified by humanitarian category, so each category has approximately the same share in all three sets. A category with too few posts to appear in all three sets is kept entirely in the training set, is left out of macro-F1, and is reported as a limitation. It is not merged with another category, because merged categories could no longer be compared with those of HUMAID-NER.

## Instruments to Be Used

Inter-annotator agreement on the humanitarian categories is measured with Cohen's kappa [@cohen1960coefficient]. Two annotators can assign the same category to a post by chance alone, so kappa removes the agreement expected by chance from the proportion of posts on which the annotators agree. A kappa of 1 means complete agreement, and a kappa of 0 means no more agreement than chance. Agreement is computed only for the categories, because the entity spans are annotated automatically by GLiNER [@zaratiana2024gliner].

Model performance refers to how correctly a model assigns humanitarian categories and marks entity spans. It is evaluated with the F1-score, which compares a model's predictions with the annotated categories and the GLiNER spans. Accuracy is not used, because the categories differ in their number of posts and a model can reach a high accuracy by favoring the most frequent categories. The F1-score combines two proportions. Precision is the proportion of a model's predictions that are correct, and recall is the proportion of the annotated items that the model finds. For a humanitarian category or an entity type $c$,
$$P_c = \frac{TP_c}{TP_c + FP_c}, \qquad R_c = \frac{TP_c}{TP_c + FN_c}, \qquad F1_c = \frac{2 P_c R_c}{P_c + R_c}$$
where $TP_c$ is the number of correct predictions of $c$, $FP_c$ is the number of incorrect predictions of $c$, $FN_c$ is the number of instances of $c$ that the model fails to predict, and $P_c$ and $R_c$ are precision and recall.

Humanitarian classification is scored with macro-F1, the mean of $F1_c$ over the ten categories. Macro-F1 gives rare categories the same weight as frequent ones. A category that is kept entirely in the training set (Section 3.3) is not part of this mean. NER is scored with span-level micro-F1, which pools the counts of all ten entity types before the formula is applied. A predicted span counts as correct only when both its boundaries and its type match those of an annotated span. Both scores are computed as in HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner].

Negative transfer occurs when a multi-task model has a lower F1-score on a task than the model trained on that task alone. It is measured as the percentage by which the F1-score of a candidate model is higher or lower than that of the single-task model. This relative change in F1-score is a widely used measure of multi-task performance [@vandenhende2022dense; @gama2026uniform]. It is computed for each task $t$ and averaged over the two tasks,
$$\Delta_t = \frac{F1_{\text{multi-task},\,t} - F1_{\text{single-task},\,t}}{F1_{\text{single-task},\,t}} \times 100\%, \qquad \Delta_{\text{MTL}} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\Delta_1 + \Delta_2\right)$$
where task 1 is humanitarian classification and task 2 is NER. Here, $F1_{\text{multi-task},\,t}$ is the F1-score of one run of a candidate model, and $F1_{\text{single-task},\,t}$ is the mean F1-score over the five runs of the single-task model for task $t$. For example, when a candidate model reaches an F1-score of 0.76 on a task and the single-task model reaches 0.80, $\Delta_t$ is −5%. A negative $\Delta_t$ indicates negative transfer on task $t$, and a positive $\Delta_t$ indicates positive transfer.

Training time is the time, in seconds, that a run spends on training steps. Peak memory is the largest amount of graphics processing unit (GPU) memory, in mebibytes, that PyTorch allocates at any moment of the run. One multi-task model replaces both single-task models, so its training time is compared with the sum of the training times of the two single-task models. Its peak memory is compared with the larger of their two peak memories, because the single-task models are trained one after the other. The overhead of an optimizer is the percentage by which the training time or peak memory of its candidate model exceeds that of the candidate model trained with equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary; @liu2023famo].

## Procedure of Data Gathering

Posts are collected through the X API, which charges US\$0.005 for each post that it returns, including posts that are later excluded [@x2026pricing]. The keywords match 176,424 posts in the collection windows (@tbl-frame-counts), so retrieving all of them would cost about US\$882. To avoid this cost, the posts are collected in two steps. First, only the number of matching posts on each day is requested, and these numbers set how many posts each day contributes to the sample. Second, the posts of each day are retrieved and filtered by the inclusion and exclusion criteria until the day has contributed its number of posts (@tbl-collection-steps). The 2,500 posts cost at least US\$12.50, and the final cost depends on how many of the retrieved posts are eligible. When fewer than 2,500 eligible posts are found, all eligible posts are annotated, and the smaller dataset is reported as a limitation.

Users of X keep ownership of their posts but grant X a license to make the posts available to others [@x2026terms]. The study receives the posts through the X API under this license, so users are not asked individually for consent. The personal information in the posts is still protected. Usernames, phone numbers, email addresses, and links are replaced with placeholders, because these details can identify a person and are not needed for either task. Names within the text of a post are kept, because PERSON is one of the entity types. The posts are stored only on the laptop used for training, and only the research group and the adjudicator have access to them. These measures follow Section 20 of the Data Privacy Act [-@philippines2012dataprivacy], which requires reasonable and appropriate measures to protect personal information against unlawful access and disclosure. As the developer policy of X requires, posts deleted on X are also deleted from the dataset, and only the post IDs are shared [@x2026devpolicy].

Two annotators assign the humanitarian category of every post in the annotation tool doccano. Both are members of the research group and are fluent in Tagalog and English. Disagreements that the annotators cannot settle are decided by an adjudicator, who comes from outside the research group and works or does research in disaster management or crisis informatics. @tbl-annotators lists the qualifications and tasks of the annotators and the adjudicator.

Annotation begins with practice batches of 50 posts. These posts are collected in the same way as the sample but are not part of it, so that no post in the sample is seen before the guidelines are fixed. After each practice batch, Cohen's kappa is computed and the guidelines in Appendix B are revised. Practice ends when kappa reaches at least .61, the lower bound of substantial agreement [@landis1977measurement], or after the third practice batch. When kappa is still below .61 after the third batch, annotation of the sample begins, and the agreement is reported as it is. The practice batches are annotated before December 2026, so they take no time from the 38 working days.

The guidelines are then fixed, and the sample is annotated from December 2026 to January 2027 in eight batches of about 310 posts, following the rules in @tbl-annotation-rules. At the planned pace of about 66 posts a day, one batch is about one working week of annotation, so agreement is measured every week. Kappa is computed for each batch from the annotations that the two annotators make independently, before any discussion. The annotators then settle their disagreements by discussion. The adjudicator, who has more knowledge of disaster response than the annotators, decides the disagreements that remain and signs off on the batch. When the kappa of a batch falls below .61, the annotators also review the guidelines and their disagreements with the adjudicator before the next batch begins. The batch is not annotated again, because the 38 working days leave no time to repeat it.

The entity spans are marked automatically by GLiNER [@zaratiana2024gliner], a pretrained NER model whose multilingual version suits posts that mix two languages. Marking every span by hand takes much longer than choosing one category, and the annotators have time only for the categories. The automatic annotation pipeline of HUMAID-NER cannot be reused, because it relies on an English language model and on rules written for English [@ali2026humaidner]. GLiNER is used without further training on the posts of the study, with the settings in @tbl-gliner-settings.

The models are trained on the training set with LibMTL [@lin2023libmtl], a library of multi-task optimizers. @tbl-training-settings lists the training settings, and @tbl-optimizer-setup lists how each optimizer is set up. Two of the settings, a batch size of 8 and an embedding layer that is not trained in any model, allow every optimizer to fit in the 8 GB of GPU memory of the laptop.

Every model is trained for 10 epochs, each of which is one pass over the training set [@warner2025modernbert]. After each epoch, the model is scored on the validation set, and the version of the model from the epoch with the highest validation score is kept [@kurin2022unitary]. The validation score of a multi-task model is the mean of its two F1-scores, and that of a single-task model is the F1-score of its task, following HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. Early stopping, which ends training once the validation score stops rising, is not used, because a comparison of multi-task optimizers should give every model the same amount of training [@xin2022mtohelp]. Class weights and oversampling are not applied either, so that the losses remain those of HUMAID-NER and the optimizer stays the only difference among the candidate models.

The learning rate, which sets the size of each update to a model, is tuned for each model, as in the reviewed comparisons of multi-task optimizers [@xin2022mtohelp; @kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform]. Each model is trained once with random seed 0 at each of the learning rates 1, 3, 5, and 8 × 10^−5^ [@warner2025modernbert], and the rate with the highest validation score is kept [@kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform]. For linear scalarization, the task weights are tuned together with the learning rate, over the values in @tbl-training-settings [@xin2022mtohelp; @royer2023scalarization].

Each model is then trained in five main runs with random seeds 1 to 5. Five runs is within the range of two to ten used in the reviewed comparisons of multi-task optimizers [@kurin2022unitary; @lin2023libmtl; @royer2023scalarization]. A random seed fixes the random choices of a run, so runs with the same seed process the training posts in the same order, regardless of the model. A run that fails, such as one that runs out of GPU memory, is repeated once with the same seed. When it fails again, the failure and its cause are reported, and the training setup is not changed for that optimizer.

A sample size based on resource constraints may not be large enough [@lakens2022sample]. To check this, each single-task model is also trained on 25%, 50%, and 75% of the training set. The resulting learning curve shows how the F1-scores change as more training posts are used [@tabuzo2026phmartiallawner]. The single-task models are used because a curve from a model that learns one task alone is not affected by the choice of multi-task optimizer. Each subset keeps the same proportions of the humanitarian categories, and a model is trained on it with seeds 1 to 5.

## Statistical Treatment

Each result is reported as the mean and sample standard deviation across the five main runs of a model. The first research question is answered with the F1-scores of the single-task models on the test set. The second is answered with the dataset and the multi-task model themselves, together with the Cohen's kappa of each batch of annotation. The third is answered with the F1-scores, relative changes, training time, and peak memory of the 13 candidate models. The F1-scores and relative changes of the candidate models are computed on the validation set, because the test set is reserved for the final model and the single-task models.

The final model is also selected on the validation set. For each of the 13 candidate models, $\Delta_{\text{MTL}}$ is averaged over the five runs, and the optimizer whose candidate model has the highest mean is used for the final model. When two candidate models have the same mean, the one with the shorter training time is selected. Among the five runs of the final model, the run with the highest validation score is used in the prototype and in the error analysis.

The fourth research question is answered on the test set, where the final model is compared with the single-task models. The hypotheses of Chapter 1 are tested with a two-sided paired t-test on the F1-scores, run once for each task. This test is appropriate because each run of the final model is paired by random seed with the single-task run that processed the training posts in the same order. The test examines whether the mean of the five differences in F1-score is zero, and the null hypothesis is rejected when $p$ is below .05. The mean difference is reported with its 95% confidence interval. The F1-score of each humanitarian category and each entity type is also reported, together with its number of posts in the test set. Training time and peak memory are compared through their means and standard deviations, without a statistical test.

## Data Analysis

The learning curve is used to judge whether the 2,500 posts are sufficient. It is interpreted by comparing adjacent training sizes, following Tabuzo et al. [-@tabuzo2026phmartiallawner], who considered a training size sufficient once a larger size no longer produced a significant gain in F1-score. This study compares the two largest sizes, 75% and 100% of the training set, because this step shows whether the F1-scores are still rising when the whole training set is used. The increase in the mean F1-score on the validation set from 75% to 100% is counted as a gain when it exceeds the standard deviation of the single-task model across its five main runs, which represents the usual variation between runs. Such a gain indicates that more posts would likely raise the F1-scores further, and this result is reported as a limitation. A smaller increase indicates that the F1-scores have stopped improving and that the 2,500 posts are sufficient. The curve of each task is interpreted separately, so the limitation may apply to one task and not the other.

The F1-scores of the final model are judged by how much they differ from those of the single-task models. No minimum acceptable F1-score is set, because no earlier study reports F1-scores for both tasks on Taglish posts about tropical cyclones. The errors of the final model are then analyzed to show which posts it misinterprets and why. No difficult posts are added to the test set on purpose, so the errors reflect the kinds of posts that the model is meant to label. For humanitarian classification, a confusion matrix shows how often each category is mistaken for each of the other categories. For NER, each incorrect span is classified by entity type and by type of error, which is a missed span, an extra span, or a span with incorrect boundaries or an incorrect type. The posts with errors are then examined together to identify what they have in common, such as their length, their mix of Tagalog and English, or their category.

## Software System Description

The software system of this study has two parts, a benchmarking system that prepares the dataset and trains, selects, and evaluates the models, and a prototype web application that presents posts labeled by the final model.

### System Structure

@fig-system-architecture is read from top to bottom. Its first two phases, data preparation and model training and selection, make up the benchmarking system, and the third phase is the prototype web application. The cylinders are stored data, and the slanted boxes are the input and output of the whole system.

The prototype has three parts, shown in the last phase of @fig-system-architecture, all of which run on the computer of the study, so the posts that the responder views are not sent to an outside service. The interface, built with React, runs in a web browser, where the responder views the labeled posts and filters them by category or entity type. The server, built with FastAPI in Python, has two roles. Before the prototype is used, the researcher starts the retrieval of new posts, in which the server requests the posts that match the search keywords from the X API, replaces their usernames, phone numbers, email addresses, and links with placeholders, as in the dataset, and labels each post with the final model. While the prototype is used, the server receives the requests from the interface and returns the matching posts from the database. The requests that the server accepts, such as a request for the posts of selected categories, are described in an API specification that FastAPI generates in the standard OpenAPI format, and the specification is kept in the GitHub repository with the code. The database, PostgreSQL, stores the posts and the labels that the final model assigned to them.

![System Architecture of the Benchmarking System and the Prototype Web Application](figures/fig-3-1-system-architecture.pdf){#fig-system-architecture}

### Use Cases

@fig-use-cases shows the actors of the prototype web application and their use cases. Before the prototype is used, the researcher retrieves new posts from X, and the prototype labels them with the final model and stores them with their humanitarian categories and entities. The responder then views and filters these labeled posts. The X API is a secondary actor, an outside system that takes part in retrieving the posts but does not start any use case. The prototype is designed for responders, but it is not deployed or tested with them (Section 3.9). @tbl-usecases groups the use cases into three categories and describes each one.

![Use Case Diagram of the Prototype Web Application](figures/fig-3-2-use-cases.pdf){#fig-use-cases}

| Use Case Category | Use Case | Use Case Description |
|:----------------|:----------------|:----------------------------------------------|
| Post Retrieval | Retrieve posts from X | Allow the researcher to start the retrieval of new posts that match the search keywords from X, which the prototype then labels with the final model and stores so that responders can view them (e.g., posts that contain *bagyo* or *baha*). |
| Post Viewing | Open the prototype | Allow responders to open the prototype in a web browser, which shows the list of posts that the final model has already labeled. |
| Post Viewing | View the labeled posts | Allow responders to see the list of all posts in the prototype, each with its text, its humanitarian category, and its highlighted entities. |
| Post Viewing | View the category of a post | Allow responders to see the humanitarian category that the final model assigned to a post (e.g., requests or urgent needs). |
| Post Viewing | View the entities of a post | Allow responders to see the entities that the final model marked in a post, each highlighted in the text with its entity type (e.g., "Brgy. Tumana, Marikina" highlighted as a location). |
| Post Filtering | Filter posts by category | Allow responders to select one or more of the ten humanitarian categories so that the list shows only the posts assigned those categories (e.g., only requests or urgent needs). |
| Post Filtering | Filter posts by entity type | Allow responders to select one or more of the ten entity types so that the list shows only the posts containing at least one entity of those types (e.g., only posts that name a location). |
| Post Filtering | Combine filters | Allow responders to select categories and entity types at the same time so that the list shows only the posts that match both (e.g., requests or urgent needs that name a location). |
| Post Filtering | Clear filters | Allow responders to remove all selected categories and entity types so that the list shows every post again. |

: Use Case Specifications {#tbl-usecases tbl-colwidths="[20,22,58]"}

In the prototype, the model only suggests the category and the entities of each post, and the responder decides which posts to act on, so an error of the model does not become a final decision.

## Testing and Evaluation

Testing checks that the software of the study works as designed. The benchmarking system is tested so that its scores and measurements are computed correctly, and the prototype is tested so that each use case works.

Testing moves from the smallest parts of the software to the whole system. Each part of the benchmarking code is tested first, then the whole benchmarking system, and finally the prototype. All tests run on the laptop in @tbl-hardware. The usability of the prototype and its performance on other computers are not tested, and the prototype is not tested with actual responders. Its use cases are instead tested by the researchers through functional testing. The benchmarking code is tested automatically with pytest, so that every test can be run again after any change to the code, and the prototype is tested by hand with written test cases. @tbl-tests summarizes what each test checks, how it is run, and when it passes.

| Test | What It Checks | How It Is Run | Pass Criterion |
|:----------------|:------------------------|:--------------------|:----------------|
| Unit testing (benchmarking code) | Each part of the code gives the correct output, from the sampling and filtering of the posts to the scores, the training cost, the statistical tests, and the 13 optimizers | Automated pytest tests on small examples worked out by hand (Appendix D) | Every output matches its hand-worked result |
| Integration testing (benchmarking system) | The parts of the code work together, from training to the result file of each run | Automated run of all 15 models on a small part of the data | Every model finishes and writes its result file |
| Functional testing (prototype) | Each of the 9 use cases works, and the prototype labels posts in the same way as the final model | Written test cases run by hand, with a stand-in for the X API (Appendix E) | The actual result matches the expected result in every test case |

: Test Summary {#tbl-tests tbl-colwidths="[18,32,28,22]"}

Before the tuning runs start, each part of the benchmarking code goes through unit testing, in which the part is run with pytest on small examples whose correct output is worked out by hand. The unit tests cover every step that produces the dataset or a result, from the sampling and filtering of the posts to the scores, the training cost, the statistical tests, and the 13 multi-task optimizers, and Appendix D lists each test. Once every part passes, integration testing runs the whole benchmarking system for all 15 models on a small part of the data, from training to the result file of each run. This test passes when every model finishes and writes its result file. When any unit or integration test fails, the code is fixed and all the tests are run again, and the tuning runs start only after every test passes.

Once the prototype is built, functional testing checks each of the 9 use cases in @tbl-usecases with at least one test case, and Appendix E lists each test case with its input, expected result, and actual result. A use case passes when the actual result matches the expected result in every test case. When a test case fails, the prototype is fixed and every test case of that use case is run again.
